opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think people underestimate how tractable it is because they've been trained to think of these problems as purely technical, as if the only lever is some clever alignment breakthrough in a lab somewhere. But when you look at history, most of the big civilizational problems we've actually made progress on weren't solved by one genius. They were solved by ordinary people deciding that something was unacceptable and then building the institutions to enforce that.

Think about nuclear weapons, ozone depletion, or the fight against tobacco companies. Each looked hopeless at first. There were powerful interests, enormous money, and a lot of people saying "this is just how things are, you can't stop progress." And yet we got treaties, regulations, and norms. Not perfectly, not cleanly, but they worked well enough to change the trajectory.

The thing about AI is that most people, when you actually explain the situation to them, get it. You don't need a PhD to understand that building systems smarter than you, which you don't understand and can't control, is a bad idea. The intuition is already there. The polling consistently shows that the public is far more concerned than the elites in tech are. So the raw material for a movement exists. What's missing is coordination, the infrastructure to turn that concern into political pressure and then into durable institutions.

And that's the part that's hard but not mysterious. We know how to do it. People have done it before. You talk to people, you organize, you make it legible to policymakers, and you build institutions that can actually hold the line over time. It's slow and unglamorous, and it doesn't feel like saving the world in the way that writing a clever paper does. But I think it's actually the thing that works.

The alternative, hoping that a handful of companies racing each other will voluntarily slow down or solve everything in time, is the truly intractable plan. So when people ask me whether this is realistic, my answer is: compared to what? Compared to doing nothing and hoping, it's by far the most realistic option we have.

r001.rationale: The response challenges reliance on a single technical breakthrough, but does not reject ideologies promising a universal remedy on the grounds that they oversimplify the world's complexity.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss physical regularities or use them to argue that the world's complexity is bounded.

r003.rationale: The response cites social and regulatory movements as precedents, but does not use the emergence of organized systems such as cells or industrial society as evidence that order can be created despite complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, so, the first thing I'd say is that I don't think it's tractable in the sense of "easy." I think it's tractable in the sense of "this is the kind of thing humans have actually done before." Like, this isn't some exotic new category of problem. We have, as a species, built institutions that constrain extremely powerful actors doing extremely dangerous things. We did it with nuclear weapons. We did it with chemical and biological weapons. We did it with ozone-depleting chemicals. None of those were clean, none of them were perfect, but they happened, and they happened because a relatively small number of people decided to take the problem seriously and then do the boring, unglamorous work of talking to other people, building coalitions, writing things down, and showing up.

And I think the AI safety community, broadly, for a long time had this kind of learned helplessness about it. There was this story that, you know, the economic incentives are just too strong, the technology is just too diffuse, the governments are too slow, so the only thing you can do is try to solve the technical alignment problem in a basement somewhere and hope you finish before the labs do. And I just think that story is wrong. Or at least, it's incomplete. It's wrong in the same way it would have been wrong in 1945 to say, "well, nuclear weapons exist now, physics is public, there's nothing anyone can do." People did things.

The second thing I'd say is that the actual bottleneck here is not that people don't care. When you go out and you talk to normal people, not AI researchers, not people on Twitter, just regular people, and you explain to them, "hey, there are a handful of companies building systems they openly say they don't understand and can't control, and they're racing each other to do it faster," the overwhelming reaction is not "that's fine." The reaction is "wait, what? Who allowed this?" Polling bears this out pretty consistently. The public is way more cautious than the industry. So the raw material for a movement is there. What's missing is organization, and organization is a skill, and skills can be learned.

And then the third thing, and this is maybe the one I feel most strongly about, is that I think the difficulty is actually an argument for doing it, not against. Because the alternative framings are worse. If you think the problem is purely technical and you just need a clever enough idea, then you're betting everything on a research breakthrough on a deadline you don't control. If you think the problem is hopeless, then you've just given up, and giving up has a one hundred percent failure rate. Whereas building institutions, building a movement, is the one path where incremental progress actually compounds. Every person you convince, every policymaker who understands the issue a little better, every norm you shift, that stays shifted. It's not a lottery ticket. It's more like building a wall one brick at a time. Each brick is small and kind of boring, but the wall is real.

So, yeah. I'm not optimistic in the sense that I think we'll definitely succeed. I'm optimistic in the sense that this is a game humans know how to play, we have the pieces, and the main thing standing between us and actually playing it is people deciding that they're allowed to.

r001.rationale: The response calls a purely technical approach incomplete, but it does not reject ideologies that promise one universal remedy or connect them to oversimplifying complexity.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim about physical regularities limiting the world's complexity.

r003.rationale: It cites previously built institutions that constrained dangerous actors as evidence that people can create organized order despite difficult problems.

astra-6.text:
I think people sometimes confuse “this is very hard” with “this is impossible.” Building a movement, getting people to coordinate, building institutions that can actually do something—these are difficult problems, but they’re recognizably human problems. We have done things like this before. You don’t need to solve some entirely new mathematical mystery to get people together and say, “Hey, we should have a say in something that could radically affect our lives.”

And you don’t need everybody to agree on every detail. People can disagree about timelines, about what intelligence is, about how the technology will develop, and still agree that companies shouldn’t be able to impose unlimited risks on everybody else without meaningful oversight. That’s a basis for cooperation.

The institutional part matters because concern alone doesn’t accomplish much. You need people who can turn that concern into sustained work: explain the problem, develop proposals, hold decision-makers accountable, and keep going when the news cycle moves on.

So I’m not saying success is guaranteed. I’m saying there are concrete things to do, and doing them can improve our position. The fact that we don’t already have institutions adequate to this problem is a reason to build them. It isn’t evidence that they can’t be built.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss ideologies or reject a single universal remedy.

r002.rationale: It does not mention physical regularities or argue that they limit the world's complexity.

r003.rationale: It says people have built movements and institutions before, but gives no example of organized systems such as cells or industrial society as evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think tractable means easy, or even that we’re likely to succeed. It means there are things we can do that plausibly make a difference. And I think people underestimate how much institutions are made of people who just decided to do something. Someone has to organize the meeting, start the organization, talk to the politician. There isn’t some other class of adults who are going to show up and handle this for us.

You also don’t need everyone to become an AI researcher. People can understand the basic proposition: companies are trying to build systems more capable than humans, and we don’t know how to reliably control those systems. You can have substantial disagreement about timelines and still think that deserves serious oversight.

A grassroots movement gives people a way to act together, and institutions give that effort continuity and expertise. Neither guarantees success. But difficulty alone doesn’t tell you that something is impossible. If the stakes are this high, and there are concrete things we can try, I think we should try them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical action and uncertainty, but does not reject ideologies that promise a single universal remedy or say they oversimplify complexity.

r002.rationale: It makes no argument about physical regularities limiting the world's complexity.

r003.rationale: It argues that people can build movements and institutions, but does not use biological cells, industrial society, or similar emergent organized systems as evidence.
